clue.text: Be similar to last of chamber group though name's forgotten

indicators.note: the final letter alone is wanted from the word that follows
a name is forgotten, so the abbreviation for name drops out of the group word

parts.note: a musical group, fitting the chamber music surface

explanation.surface: A chamber ensemble plays on, though one member's name has been forgotten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group' is the musical kind, in keeping with the chamber music surface; N is the usual abbreviation for name.
explanation.definitionFit: To resemble someone is to look or behave like them, a straightforward verb synonym.

clue.text: Character in computer game about King getting quick look?

indicators.note: one thing placed about another wraps around it

parts.note: a Sim is a person in the computer game The Sims
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A video game figure meets a king and gets a brief glimpse.
explanation.walkthrough: SIM goes about K to give SKIM.
explanation.definitionFit: To skim a page is to read through it rapidly, glancing over it without attention to detail.

clue.text: Pageantry linked to high award or decoration

parts.note: the Order of Merit, a senior British honour

explanation.surface: Ceremonial splendour goes along with top honours and medals.
explanation.walkthrough: The OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour limited to a few dozen members.
explanation.definitionFit: A pompom is a woolly ball used to ornament hats and cheerleaders' outfits, a kind of trimming.

clue.text: Waste container readily inscribed with name of former PM

indicators.note: a surface inscribed with words carries them within it

parts.note: as in 'I would as soon go', meaning as readily
William Pitt, elder or younger, both British prime ministers

explanation.surface: A rubbish bin is promptly engraved with the name of an ex-premier.
explanation.walkthrough: Pitt the Elder and Pitt the Younger were both 18th-century British prime ministers; 'as soon' means 'as readily'.
explanation.definitionFit: A spittoon is a receptacle for people to spit into, literally a vessel for bodily waste.

clue.text: Revolting? Our bellies may be turned

indicators.note: something turned is churned about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something disgusting is enough to make our stomachs churn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolting' reads as disgusting, matching the queasy bellies, but it means rising in revolt.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebels are in revolt against authority, so revolting in the uprising sense matches the adjective.

clue.text: A policy about power as seen in Southern European area?

definitions.text: as seen in Southern European area?

indicators.note: the policy word goes about the next item, enclosing it

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for power

explanation.surface: A policy on electricity supply in a region of southern Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: A, then P placed inside LINE: A LINE around P.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps form a mountain region of southern Europe, so anything found there can be described with this adjective.

clue.text: Minor ache around back of neck for seven days

indicators.note: the ache word goes around the next item, enclosing it

parts.note: to ache for something is to long for it

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A slight pain at the back of the neck that lasts a whole week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ache' looks like a noun beside 'minor', but it is the verb, as in aching for home.
explanation.definitionFit: Something weeklong lasts throughout one week, which is a span of seven days.

clue.text: Good move to surface seeing capture of lake salmon

indicators.note: a capture holds its prisoner inside, so the lake abbreviation is enclosed

parts.note: to rise is to come up to the surface

explanation.surface: A fish rising to the surface of a lake is caught: a good result.
explanation.walkthrough: A grilse is a young salmon returning from the sea for the first time.
explanation.definitionFit: A grilse is a young salmon that has spent only one winter at sea before coming back to fresh water.

clue.text: A large interval — taken aback — for stew to appear

indicators.note: something taken aback is pushed backwards, so the run of letters goes right to left

parts.note: L is the clothing size abbreviation for large
a leap is a jump, an interval between musical notes

explanation.surface: Someone is startled by a long gap before the stew is served.
explanation.walkthrough: A L LEAP reads backwards as PAELLA. In music a leap is an interval wider than a step.
explanation.definitionFit: Paella is a Spanish rice dish cooked slowly with meat or seafood, loosely a stew.

clue.text: Direct line contributing to border

indicators.note: a line contributing to the border is put into it, so it sits inside

parts.note: a hem is the edge of a piece of cloth

explanation.surface: Sewing a straight line into the edging of a garment.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes inside HEM to give HELM.
explanation.definitionFit: To helm something is to steer it, like a ship's wheel, so it means to direct or lead.

clue.text: Newspapers etc misrepresented maiden trip

indicators.note: a misrepresented account is distorted, so these letters are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: The press gave a distorted report of a first voyage.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers and magazines are the printed means of mass communication, as opposed to broadcast or online channels.

clue.text: I remain moored at the outset in the same place

parts.note: to bide is to stay put

indicators.note: the outset of a word is its opening letter only

explanation.surface: A boat-owner says they are staying tied up at their usual spot.
explanation.walkthrough: IBIDEM is the Latin used in footnotes, often shortened to ibid., to cite the source just mentioned.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word literally translates as in the same place, used in references to repeat a citation.

clue.text: Upturn in cold lives sadly ending in poverty? Definitely

indicators.note: in a down entry an upturned word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: something iced is put in the cold

indicators.note: things going sadly are going wrong, so the letters are put out of order
the ending of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: An economic upturn among people living in the cold and in poverty, emphatically.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting decisively means settling matters conclusively, so the adverb conveys certainty, like definitely.

clue.text: First serving of strawberry crumble to appear still warm?

indicators.note: the first part served of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: to moulder is to decay and crumble away

explanation.surface: A strawberry crumble pudding served while it is still warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crumble' looks like the pudding but is a verb meaning decay.
explanation.definitionFit: Embers smoulder when they burn slowly without flame, still giving off heat after the fire dies down.

clue.text: Ancient British soldier in left-wing Ulster?

parts.note: red is the colour of socialism
an ulster is a long, heavy overcoat

explanation.surface: A historic British soldier serving in Northern Ireland, with a political twist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ulster' suggests the Irish province but here is the long overcoat named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Redcoat was the old nickname for a British Army soldier, from the scarlet tunics worn in earlier centuries.

clue.text: Snake study accepted by Commonwealth country? Not initially

indicators.note: something accepted by another is taken inside it
the opening letter is not there, so it is dropped

parts.note: to con is to study or learn

explanation.surface: A study of snakes carried out in a Commonwealth nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' is the old verb con, to learn by heart; the leading letter goes only after the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: The anaconda is a very large South American constricting serpent, a specific example of the reptile.

clue.text: Laudatory remarks? End one about college, retiring

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the whole string runs backwards

parts.note: an end is a goal or aim

indicators.note: the number word goes about the next item, enclosing it

explanation.surface: Speeches praising a college figure who is retiring at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Retiring applies to the whole string built so far. Encomia is the plural of encomium.
explanation.definitionFit: An encomium is a formal speech or text of high praise, so the plural means laudatory tributes.

clue.text: Painful nail? Odd thing to involve dispute

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it inside
something odd is out of the ordinary, so its letters are arranged strangely

explanation.surface: A sore nail is a strange thing to cause an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange THING as ING-TH and put ROW in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingrowing toenail curls into the flesh; the noun names that growth inward, here the sore result.

clue.text: Recording device starts to ruin every part of speech

indicators.note: the starts of the words are their opening letters only

parts.note: first letters of ruin and every
a verb is a grammatical class

explanation.surface: A recording machine wrecks every bit of a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of speech' sounds like a fragment of an address but is a grammar term.
explanation.definitionFit: Reverb, short for reverberation, is an echo effect or the studio unit that adds it to recorded sound.

clue.text: Winter sports item that is catching cold fish

indicators.note: what catches something holds it inside

parts.note: i.e., the Latin abbreviation id est
C for cold, as on taps
a skate is a flat fish

explanation.surface: Winter gear that is used for catching fish through the ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' looks like the thing caught, but it is the flatfish that ends the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice skate is a boot with a blade for gliding on frozen surfaces, kit for a cold-weather pastime.

clue.text: Pink binding for Beethoven's Fifth or Ninth?

indicators.note: something binding another wraps tightly around it
the fifth letter of the composer's name is the one kept

explanation.surface: A pink cover for a recording of a Beethoven symphony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fifth' and 'Ninth' look like symphonies; one counts letters. Beethoven's Ninth is nicknamed the Choral Symphony.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's Ninth Symphony is called the Choral because its finale uses singers, so the question mark marks an example.

clue.text: Have joint responsibility for authorising function, by the sound of it

indicators.note: the wordplay is judged by how the word is heard, not spelt

parts.note: the cosine is a trigonometric function

explanation.surface: A sharing of duty for authorising some official role.
explanation.definitionFit: To co-sign a document is to add a second signature, so two people share accountability for its approval.

clue.text: Sickeningly attractive copper still upset about end of murderess

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: in a down entry upset means turned upside down, so read upwards
the still word goes about the next piece, enclosing it

parts.note: yet and still both mean even now

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A policeman is still shaken by the fate of a killer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a police officer but is the metal's symbol. S goes inside YET, then the whole is reversed after CU.
explanation.definitionFit: Cutesy describes something affectedly or excessively pretty, cuteness laid on so thick it cloys.

clue.text: Peaceful action forbidden before church season — six apprehended

indicators.note: something apprehended is caught and held inside

parts.note: a no-no is something not allowed

explanation.surface: Something banned before Lent, with six people arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Action forbidden' is a single idea, the informal no-no, not a definition plus wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-violent protest avoids force or harm, so the adjective describes a calm, pacific approach.

clue.text: Offload fire's foremost source of fuel

indicators.note: the foremost letter of a word is its first

parts.note: a log is burnt as fuel

explanation.surface: Unloading the main supply of firewood.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, to flog is to sell something off.
explanation.definitionFit: Flog in informal British usage means sell, a way to get rid of goods you no longer want.

clue.text: Elevated halo often seen around this simpleton?

indicators.note: in a down entry elevated means lifted up, so read from the bottom
the letters are seen in the words around them, spread across two

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A saintly halo often surrounds this innocent simpleton.
explanation.walkthrough: haLO OFten holds LOOF, which read upwards gives FOOL.
explanation.definitionFit: A fool is a silly or foolish person, a plain synonym for a simple-minded dupe.

clue.text: Attempt to snatch a type of light? That gets you imprisoned

indicators.note: what snatches something holds it inside its grasp

parts.note: to have a go is to make an attempt

explanation.surface: Trying to steal a lamp is a way to get locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: Gaol is the British spelling of jail.
explanation.definitionFit: To be gaoled is to be put in prison, using the older British spelling of jailed.

clue.text: Italian treats in Book Two about romantic novelist

indicators.note: the numeral goes about the novelist, enclosing him

parts.note: Sir Walter Scott, author of Ivanhoe

explanation.surface: The second volume of a romance features sweet delicacies from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Romantic here means of the Romantic movement: Sir Walter Scott wrote Ivanhoe and Waverley.
explanation.definitionFit: Biscotti are twice-baked almond biscuits from Italy, hard sweet snacks often dipped in coffee.
